passage_text: Researchers investigated the effect of different auditory cues on cognitive performance during a sustained attention task. Twenty-four healthy adults (12 males, 12 females, age 22–35) were randomly assigned to one of four groups: Control (no cue), Condition A (continuous low‑frequency tone), Condition B (intermittent high‑frequency tone), and Condition C (continuous white noise). Each participant completed a 30‑minute vigilance task while their reaction times to target stimuli were recorded. The mean reaction time (RT) and standard deviation (SD) for each group are presented in Table 1. The researchers hypothesized that auditory cues would reduce RT variability, thereby improving sustained attention. Data analysis revealed that Condition A produced the fastest mean RT, followed by Condition C, Condition B, and the Control group. Despite the faster mean RT, Condition B exhibited the largest SD, suggesting increased inconsistency. The authors noted that the low‑frequency tone was associated with the fastest mean RT and the smallest SD, although no statistical test was reported, and they suggested future studies examine neural correlates using EEG.
table_data:
Condition | Mean RT (ms) | SD
Control | 350 | 30
Condition A | 320 | 25
Condition B | 340 | 35
Condition C | 330 | 28
stem: Which condition had the lowest mean reaction time?
explanation: The table shows Condition A had a mean RT of 320 ms, the lowest among all groups.
trap: Choosing the Control group or another condition without comparing all four means; the lowest mean reaction time is Condition A's 320 ms.

stem: Which factor was manipulated in this experiment?
explanation: The independent variable was the type of auditory cue presented to participants.
trap: Mistaking participant characteristics or task length for the manipulated variable; only the auditory cue type was varied.

stem: What is the difference in mean reaction time between Condition A and the Control group?
trap: Subtracting the wrong pair of means gives 10, 20 or 40 ms; the control minus Condition A is 350 − 320 = 30 ms.

stem: Which of the following is NOT a valid interpretation of the data?

options.A: Condition A had a lower mean RT than the Control group.
options.D: Condition B has the largest SD.

explanation: Correct: B) Condition B had the largest SD (35 ms, versus 30 ms for Control), so its variability was higher, not lower. Why the others are wrong: A) 320 ms is lower than the Control mean of 350 ms. C) Condition C's SD (28 ms) is below the Control SD (30 ms). D) Condition B's SD of 35 ms is the largest of the four groups.
trap: Reading a larger SD as lower variability; a larger SD means more spread, so the claim that Condition B reduces variability is the misinterpretation.

stem: Which statement about Table 1 is supported by the data?

options.A: Every auditory cue condition had a lower mean RT than the Control group.
options.B: Every auditory cue condition had a lower SD than the Control group.
options.C: Condition B had the lowest mean RT of the three cue conditions.
options.D: Condition C had the largest SD of all four groups.

explanation: Correct: Control mean RT was 350 ms, and Conditions A, B and C were 320, 340 and 330 ms, all lower. Why the others are wrong: B) Condition B had SD 35, higher than the Control SD of 30. C) Condition B (340 ms) had the highest mean RT of the three cue conditions, not the lowest. D) Condition B (SD 35) had the largest SD; Condition C was 28.
trap: Assuming every cue helped on every measure; Condition B had a higher SD than Control (35 vs 30 ms), so the claim that every condition lowered SD fails.
